lesson_title: Day 7 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 6 (Day 6 lessons and the Bitcoin trace lab: attribution, clustering, ransomware, heuristics and confidence)

lectures.title: Bitcoin trace lab: following a ransom to the first service

questions.question_stem: A ransom trace shows one transaction spending two ransom addresses as inputs. What do you write for the link?
questions.correct_answer: Co-spend: one wallet holds both addresses; it fails if the transaction is a CoinJoin; Moderate.
incorrect_answers: Co-spend: one wallet holds both addresses; it cannot fail, because inputs need one key; High.
Change clue: the second input is the change; it fails if the wallet is a CoinJoin; Moderate.
Co-spend: the two addresses belong to the payer and the payee; it fails on a reuse; Low.
questions.explanation: A trace entry names the heuristic, the known false positive and a confidence on the course scale. Co-spend assumes one wallet signed every input, and a CoinJoin is where that fails. Here the outputs are two unlike amounts, not an equal-output shape, so Moderate stands.

questions.question_stem: A transaction pays 0.5 BTC to a P2SH address and 1.512279 BTC to a P2WPKH address, like the input. Why does the change call stop at Moderate?
questions.correct_answer: Script type and round amount both come from one transaction, so they count as one kind of evidence.
incorrect_answers: The two clues contradict each other, so they cancel out and leave only a guess at the change.
Moderate is the lowest word on the scale, so any call about a change output has to use that one word.
A round amount marks the change, so the clue is certain but the script type adds some doubt.
questions.explanation: High needs two or more independent kinds of evidence with no known failure. Type and amount of outputs of the same transaction are one kind, and a wallet that pays an un-round amount to a P2WPKH address would defeat both. Moderate is the ceiling here.
questions.lesson_block: Why clues from one transaction stop at Moderate

questions.question_stem: Three hops each pay a round amount to a non-P2WPKH address and roll an un-round remainder to a new P2WPKH address. What is the pattern, and how do you record the peels?
questions.correct_answer: A peel chain; record each peel as a lead with its next transaction, as an exchange's withdrawals look the same.
incorrect_answers: A CoinJoin; record each peel as the attacker's wallet, because steps that look alike show only one owner.
A peel chain; record each peel as the attacker's wallet, because the repeat of the pattern settles exactly who owns it.
A batch payout; record the remainder as a lead, because one input can feed many different payees in one go.
questions.explanation: A peel chain peels a payment off and rolls the remainder forward. The pattern is regular, but an exchange's withdrawals look alike, and a regular pattern is one kind of evidence. So the peels are leads, each followed to its next transaction, at Moderate.

questions.question_stem: A transaction has 12 inputs, 11 of which received once from different earlier transactions, and one output of 2.5178 BTC. Is it a sweep or a CoinJoin?
questions.correct_answer: A sweep: one output of one amount is not a CoinJoin's equal-output shape; a service gathering deposits fits.
incorrect_answers: A CoinJoin: twelve inputs from separate sources are what a mixing round looks like here to an analyst.
A CoinJoin: a service that gathers coins from separate sources pays them out as equal outputs, so it mixes them.
A sweep: the single output belongs to the thief, so the 11 other inputs are the thief's own deposits.
questions.explanation: A CoinJoin has several equal outputs, so that its coins cannot be matched one to one. One output of one amount cannot hide who owns what; co-spend then says one wallet holds all 12 inputs. The chain does not say which service. The lab rates it Moderate.

questions.question_stem: The trail ends at a transaction with 1 input and 14 outputs, 13 to different addresses. What do you report?
questions.correct_answer: A batch payout by a service, so the trail has reached it; the chain cannot name it, and the call is Low until labelled.
incorrect_answers: A CoinJoin round, so the trail stops here; all 14 outputs are equally likely to be the attacker's, with no way to choose.
A peel chain with 13 peels, so the trail goes on; the 14th output is the change, and so it holds all of the ransom that is left.
A batch payout by the attacker, so the 13 recipients are accomplices; the call is High on the shape of the payout alone.
questions.explanation: One input paying many addresses is payment batching, which exchanges and other services use. The recipients are other people's addresses, so the trace ends. A business or a mixer batches too, and without a source label the pattern alone is Low.

questions.question_stem: Why does one false link in a cluster matter so much?
questions.correct_answer: Clusters grow by chaining, so one wrong link merges two whole actors into one, as in Meiklejohn's super-cluster.
incorrect_answers: It corrects itself at the next co-spend, because later evidence always contradicts a wrong link in time.
It affects only the two addresses it joins, because a cluster stops growing at an error it meets in the data.
It does nothing, because a link from a change guess is Low and Low links are not used for clusters later on.
questions.explanation: If A and B co-spend and B and C co-spend, all three join. A single wrong link therefore fuses two whole clusters; a huge cluster is usually a service. Writing down each link's heuristic lets a bad one be found and cut.

specific_source.reading: One false link merges two actors into one

questions.question_stem: A transaction has two outputs and the change clues do not separate them. What do you write?
incorrect_answers: The larger output, taken as change, at Moderate.
The fresh-address output, taken as change, at High.
Neither output: end the whole trace at this point.
questions.explanation: One clue is Low, several agreeing are Moderate, and when the clues do not separate the outputs the honest call is 'change undetermined': follow both rather than pick one.

specific_source.reading: Two outputs aren't always payment and change

questions.question_stem: The Colonial ransom trace in the FBI affidavit ends at a holding address of about 69.6 BTC. What do you report?
questions.correct_answer: That the trace stopped at a holding address, not at a service, and the date you checked it.
incorrect_answers: That the trace reached an exchange, since an address gathering coins from many others is a service.
That the trace is incomplete, since a ransom trace only counts once it ends at a service.
That the coins were mixed, since an address that stops moving shows the funds were laundered.
questions.explanation: The affidavit's trace ends at an address holding the coins, never at a service. Report where it stopped and what that means, with the as-of date, and do not claim a cash-out the chain does not show.

specific_source.reading: This trace stopped at a wallet, not a service

questions.question_stem: Two analytics platforms both cluster an address to the same exchange. What confidence does that give?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate, because two platforms running clustering heuristics are one kind of evidence.
incorrect_answers: High, because two tools that agree are the standard for independent lines of evidence.
Low, because a platform tag whose basis you cannot see is always an unverified one.
High, but only if the two platforms are made by different vendors and use other data, in total.
questions.explanation: Confidence counts kinds of evidence, not tools. Two platforms agreeing is one kind (clustering): Moderate. A cluster plus a label of another kind, such as an owner's listing, is what reaches High.

specific_source.reading: Attribution confidence: count kinds of evidence

questions.question_stem: An explorer tags a cluster 'Exchange X' and shows no basis for the tag. How much does that tag count for on its own?
questions.correct_answer: Low: one unverified label, because a label is only as good as its source and you cannot see how they knew.
incorrect_answers: Moderate, because an explorer reviews its tags before it publishes them for all of its many readers.
High, because a label is evidence of a different kind from the clustering it sits on top of, here.
None, because a tag with no basis shown is never allowed to count as evidence in any finding that you write.
questions.explanation: Ask of each label who says so, how they knew and how it could be wrong. One tag of unknown basis is Low; an owner's or government's listing for the exact address is Moderate; a cluster plus a label of another kind can reach High.
questions.lesson_block: A label is only as good as its source

specific_source.reading: A label is only as good as its source

questions.question_stem: A DarkSide ransom of 75 BTC splits into about 11.25 BTC and 63.75 BTC, paid to separate wallets. What does the split most likely show, and how sure can you be?
questions.correct_answer: The developer's cut and the affiliate's share; Low, since it rests on the amount alone.
incorrect_answers: The developer's cut and the affiliate's share; High, since Elliptic published the rates.
A payment and its change; Moderate, since the smaller output goes to a brand-new address.
Two affiliates who split the ransom between them; Moderate, since the wallets are separate.
questions.explanation: In ransomware-as-a-service the developer takes a share of each ransom from the affiliate who ran the attack, and the shares go to separate wallets. About 15% fits a developer's cut, but Elliptic's rates do not cover a ransom of this size (about $4.3 million), and no record says which output was whose: amount alone is Low.

specific_source.reading: Developer and affiliate split it on-chain

questions.question_stem: Your ransom trace reaches an address OFAC listed for the Hydra darknet market. What has the trace reached?
questions.correct_answer: A service: a market that sold ransomware tools and was also a route to cash out at exchanges.
incorrect_answers: The affiliate's own wallet, since a darknet market keeps no pooled addresses used by others.
A dead end, since Tor hides a market's payments on the blockchain as well as its users.
A mixer, since a darknet market exists to break the link between the payer and the payee.
questions.explanation: A darknet market is a shop and a cash-out. Hydra sold ransomware-as-a-service and other illegal goods, and most of the illicit bitcoin Russian exchanges received directly in 2019 came from it. Tor hides users, not the coins: Treasury notes that users wrongly think the coins can't be traced.

specific_source.reading: A darknet market is a shop and a cash-out

questions.question_stem: In Bitcoin Fog, OSINT (an alias and forum posts) pointed to the person behind the mixer. How far does that OSINT carry on its own?
questions.correct_answer: It is a lead to a person or a service, and it needs another line of evidence.
incorrect_answers: It gives High confidence, because forum posts are public and anyone can check them.
It counts for nothing, because off-chain sources cannot bear on on-chain work.
It is as strong as a government listing, because the operator wrote those posts.
questions.explanation: OSINT, information anyone can read such as forum posts and websites, is a lead that needs another line. In Bitcoin Fog the person came from the alias, forum activity and an IP analysis, all off the chain, and those records together, not one post, named him.

specific_source.reading: A label is only as good as its source

questions.question_stem: An agent reads your five-part explanation of a mixer trace and asks why it never names who ran the mixer. Which part should already have answered that?
questions.correct_answer: Part 5, what it cannot show: who ran it came from records off the chain, not from the trace.
incorrect_answers: Part 3, what is inferred: the person is the last step of clustering, so it belongs there.
Part 4, how confident: the person is named once the confidence word has reached High.
Part 1, the bottom line: a reader who reads one line must learn there that no one is named.
questions.explanation: The model explanation has five parts in plain words: bottom line, what the chain shows, what is inferred, how confident, and what it cannot show. For Bitcoin Fog, part 5 says who ran it came from records off the chain, and that the address count is a floor. The analyst's assessment ends at what the evidence shows.
